h1: Sports Medicine Podiatrist in Kirkland, WA
summary: Our Kirkland sports medicine podiatrists help runners, soccer players, hikers, cyclists, skiers and weekend athletes find the cause of foot and ankle pain and build a plan to keep moving.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Runners, soccer players, hikers, cyclists and skiers

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Foot, heel, ankle or shin pain during activity

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: An exam with a gait and biomechanics review

overview: If foot or ankle pain keeps you from your sport, a sports medicine podiatrist in Kirkland, WA can help. Sports medicine podiatry looks at how your feet, ankles and legs handle the stress of training. At Run Doctor, we treat runners, soccer players, hikers, cyclists, skiers and weekend athletes. You do not have to be an elite athlete. If pain changes how you move or what you love to do, it is worth a look.

Dr. Lawrence Maurer is a foot and ankle surgeon who runs, skis and mountain bikes. Dr. Kate Cryderman grew up in Kirkland, played college sports and has a special interest in sports medicine and biomechanics. Both understand how hard it is to sit out. They know most athletes want a plan that gets them back to activity safely, not just a quick fix for the day.

We start with conservative care. That can include activity changes, strength and mobility work, better footwear, taping or bracing, and custom orthotics when they make sense. We also study your gait, on video or in person. Surgery is only discussed when it is the best option or when other care has not helped. Patients visit us from Kirkland, Totem Lake, Bellevue, Redmond, Woodinville, Bothell and Seattle.
symptoms: Pain in the heel, arch, forefoot or ankle that starts or gets worse with activity
Pain in the shin or calf during or after a run
Swelling or bruising after a twist, fall or hard landing
Stiffness in the first steps after rest, or in the morning
Pain that forces you to cut a workout short or skip it
A feeling that the ankle is weak or gives way
Pain that returns every time you build up mileage or training time

causes.title: Training errors
causes.text: Adding mileage, speed, hills or jumping too fast is a common reason for overuse injuries. Tissues need time to adapt, and pain often shows up when the load grows faster than the body can handle.

causes.title: Foot structure and alignment
causes.text: Flat feet, high arches and other alignment patterns can change how force travels through the foot, ankle, shin and knee. Over many miles or games, that extra stress may add up.

causes.title: Movement patterns
causes.text: The way you land, push off or pedal affects which tissues take the load. Small changes in stride, cadence or posture may raise strain on one area, such as the Achilles tendon or the arch.

causes.title: Footwear and equipment
causes.text: Worn running shoes, stiff ski boots, cleats that do not fit or cycling shoes with poor support can all add stress. Gear that does not match your foot may be part of the problem.

causes.title: Past injuries and weakness
causes.text: An old ankle sprain, weak hips, a tight calf or limited ankle motion may change how you move. Your body may then overload another area without you noticing at first.

diagnosis: Your visit starts with a talk about your sport, your training, your shoes and when the pain began. Then we examine your feet and ankles, check strength, flexibility and joint motion, and look at your alignment while you stand and move. Gait analysis, on video or in person, shows how you walk or run. We may order an X-ray or other imaging when the exam points to a bone, joint or tendon problem. You leave with a clear explanation and a plan that fits your goals and your calendar.

treatments.title: Activity changes and smart rest
treatments.text: We often adjust your training instead of stopping it. That may mean less mileage, softer surfaces or cross training. The goal is to calm the injury while you stay as active as is safe.

treatments.title: Strength and mobility work
treatments.text: Targeted exercises for the calf, foot, hip and ankle may help your body handle load better. We explain what to do, how often, and how to build back up in steps.

treatments.title: Footwear advice
treatments.text: We help you choose shoes, boots or cleats that fit your foot shape and your sport. Sometimes a change in shoe type or lacing can make a real difference in comfort.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics
treatments.text: When foot mechanics are part of the problem, custom orthotics may help support the foot and spread out stress. They are made from a scan or cast of your own feet.

treatments.title: Taping, bracing and in-office care
treatments.text: Taping, braces or other supports may protect an injured area while it heals. We also use hands-on and other in-office treatments when they fit your diagnosis.

treatments.title: Surgery when it is the best option
treatments.text: Surgery is not our first step. It may be discussed if a structural problem needs it or if months of conservative care have not helped. Dr. Maurer is a foot and ankle surgeon.

whenToSeeUs: Pain lasts more than a week or two, even with rest
Pain keeps getting worse or returns every time you train
You can feel swelling, bruising or a sudden pop after an injury
Your ankle keeps rolling or feels unstable
You are training for a race or season and want to prevent problems
prevention: Build mileage, speed and hills in small steps instead of big jumps
Replace worn shoes and use gear that fits your foot and sport
Mix in strength work for the calves, feet, hips and core
Warm up before activity and vary your surfaces
Pay attention to early aches and get them checked before they grow

faqs.q: What does a sports medicine podiatrist do?
faqs.a: A sports medicine podiatrist treats foot, ankle and lower leg problems linked to activity. We find why the pain started, look at your shoes, training and movement, and build a plan. Care often includes exercise, footwear advice, bracing or orthotics. Surgery is only one option, and it is not the first step.

faqs.q: Do I need to be an athlete to see a sports podiatrist?
faqs.a: No, you do not need to be an athlete. Weekend hikers, casual runners, recreational soccer players and anyone who walks a lot can benefit. If foot or ankle pain limits something you enjoy, a sports medicine visit may help you understand the cause and find a way back to activity.

faqs.q: Can I keep running while I heal?
faqs.a: Sometimes yes, but it depends on the injury. Some problems allow reduced mileage or cross training, while others, such as a possible stress fracture, may need rest. We examine the area first, then give you a clear plan so you can stay active in a safe way.

faqs.q: How do I find a sports medicine podiatrist in Kirkland, WA?
faqs.a: Look for a podiatrist with a special interest in sports medicine and biomechanics. Run Doctor is in Kirkland near Totem Lake. Dr. Maurer and Dr. Cryderman both treat active people. You can call 425-899-3234 to book. We see patients from across the Eastside and Seattle.

faqs.q: Will I need surgery for a sports injury?
faqs.a: Most foot and ankle sports injuries are first treated without surgery. Rest, load changes, exercises, footwear changes, bracing and orthotics help many people. Surgery may be discussed if a problem is structural, severe, or has not improved with good conservative care. We explain every option before you decide.

title: Custom Orthotics
metaTitle: Custom Orthotics for Athletes in Kirkland, WA | Run Doctor
metaDescription: Learn how custom orthotics in Kirkland, WA differ from store-bought inserts. Scan or cast based support for your feet. Call Run Doctor to book an exam.
summary: Custom orthotics are shoe inserts made from a scan or cast of your feet. They may help support and balance your feet when pain is linked to how they move. We help you decide if they fit.

quickFacts.label: Made from
quickFacts.value: A scan or cast of your own feet

quickFacts.label: Often used for
quickFacts.value: Heel, arch, forefoot and overuse pain

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: A foot exam and gait review

overview: Custom orthotics in Kirkland, WA are shoe inserts made for one person. They are not the same as the soft inserts sold in a store. A podiatrist first finds out why your foot hurts. If foot mechanics are part of the cause, an orthotic may help support the foot and spread out stress. They are one tool, and they are not right for every problem.

Store-bought inserts are made in standard shapes and sizes. Some people find them helpful, especially for mild cushioning. A custom orthotic is made from a scan or cast of your feet and from what we learn in your exam and gait review. The shape, firmness and materials can be matched to your foot, your shoes and your activity. This is why a custom device may fit better than a shelf product.

At Run Doctor, we try conservative care first and use orthotics when they make sense. Dr. Maurer and Dr. Cryderman treat runners, hikers, cyclists, skiers and everyday walkers. Patients come from Kirkland, Bellevue, Redmond, Bothell and nearby. We explain what we expect orthotics to do, how long to break them in, and when to check back. Bring your usual shoes to your visit so we can plan around them.
symptoms: Heel or arch pain that builds during walking, standing or running
Pain along the inside or outside of the foot or ankle
Shoes that wear down quickly on one side
Sore balls of the feet or pain under the forefoot
Knee, hip or shin pain that may be linked to how the foot moves
Tired, aching feet after short activity
Store-bought inserts that have not helped enough

causes.title: Flat or low arches
causes.text: When the arch lowers a lot during standing or walking, the foot may roll inward. This can add strain to the arch, heel, shin and knee, and an orthotic may help support the foot.

causes.title: High, stiff arches
causes.text: A high arch may not absorb shock well. Pressure can build in the heel and forefoot. A well-made orthotic may help spread that pressure over a larger area of the foot.

causes.title: Overuse during sport
causes.text: Running, hiking and court sports repeat the same load again and again. If the foot is not well supported, certain tissues may take extra stress and become painful over time.

causes.title: Uneven foot motion
causes.text: Some feet move too much or too little as they land and push off. A biomechanical exam helps show which pattern you have, and that guides the design of the orthotic.

causes.title: Ill-fitting or worn shoes
causes.text: Even a good orthotic works best in a shoe that fits well. Worn out shoes or shoes with the wrong shape can add stress, so we review your footwear during the visit.

diagnosis: Orthotics start with a diagnosis, not a device. We ask about your pain, your activities and your shoes. Then we do a biomechanical exam, checking foot shape, joint motion, strength and alignment while you stand, walk and sometimes run. Gait analysis helps us see how your foot behaves in motion. If an orthotic is a good fit, we take a scan or cast of your feet and note your goals. Imaging may be used if the exam points to another problem. We then explain the plan and what to expect.

treatments.title: Scan or cast based custom orthotics
treatments.text: We capture the shape of your feet with a scan or cast. The orthotic is then made for your feet, your shoes and your sport. Firmness and shape are chosen to match your needs.

treatments.title: Fitting and break-in guidance
treatments.text: New orthotics often feel different at first. We show you how to wear them in slowly, which shoes work best and what to watch for. We check how they feel and adjust the plan.

treatments.title: Shoe selection advice
treatments.text: The right shoe helps an orthotic do its job. We discuss shoe shape, depth and support so your orthotics fit well and feel comfortable in your daily and sport shoes.

treatments.title: Exercises and strengthening
treatments.text: Orthotics often work best alongside exercises for the foot, calf and hip. We may give you simple moves that help your body handle load and support the work of the orthotic.

treatments.title: Other conservative care
treatments.text: Depending on your diagnosis, we may also suggest activity changes, taping, bracing or other in-office care. Orthotics are one part of a larger plan, not a stand-alone answer.

treatments.title: Follow-up and adjustments
treatments.text: We check back to see how you are doing. If your pain, shoes or activity change, the plan can change too. In some cases, we may suggest a different orthotic design.

whenToSeeUs: Foot or heel pain has lasted more than a couple of weeks
Store-bought inserts have not given enough relief
You have pain in the foot, shin, knee or hip that may link to foot mechanics
Your shoes wear unevenly or fast
You want help choosing the right kind of support before a race or season
prevention: Replace worn shoes and inserts on a regular schedule
Choose shoes that fit the shape and width of your feet
Break in new orthotics slowly, as advised
Keep your calves, feet and hips strong and flexible
Get new foot pain checked before it becomes a longer problem

faqs.q: What is the difference between custom orthotics and store-bought inserts?
faqs.a: Custom orthotics are made from a scan or cast of your own feet and from a full exam. Store-bought inserts come in standard sizes and shapes. Some people do well with off-the-shelf inserts, but custom devices can be matched to your foot, your shoes and your activity.

faqs.q: How do I know if I need custom orthotics?
faqs.a: The best way is an exam. Orthotics may help if foot pain is linked to arch shape, foot motion or overuse, or if store-bought inserts have not helped enough. Many foot problems get better with other care, so we decide what fits you before suggesting any device.

faqs.q: Are custom orthotics in Kirkland made from a scan or a cast?
faqs.a: Custom orthotics can be made from either a digital scan or a cast of your feet. Both capture the shape of your foot so the device can be built for you. We explain the process at your visit and choose the method that suits your needs.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get used to orthotics?
faqs.a: Most people need a short break-in period, and it varies from person to person. We often suggest wearing them for a short time each day, then adding more. Mild awareness is common at first. If you have pain or rubbing, call us so we can check the fit.

faqs.q: Can I use orthotics in running shoes, hiking boots and ski boots?
faqs.a: Often yes, but the shoe must have enough room. Orthotics can be made thinner or shaped for different footwear, such as running shoes, cleats or boots. Tell us which shoes you use most so we can plan the design and check that everything fits well.

title: Biomechanics & Gait Analysis
metaTitle: Gait Analysis and Biomechanics in Kirkland, WA | Run Doctor
metaDescription: Get gait analysis in Kirkland, WA with a full biomechanical exam. Video and in person review helps explain foot, ankle and leg pain. Book a visit with us.
h1: Gait Analysis and Biomechanics in Kirkland, WA
summary: Gait analysis and a biomechanical exam show how your feet, ankles and legs move when you walk or run. This helps explain pain and guides care, such as exercises, footwear and orthotics.

quickFacts.label: Includes
quickFacts.value: Video and in person gait review, plus a physical exam

quickFacts.label: Helpful for
quickFacts.value: Runners, walkers and anyone with repeat foot pain

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Book a biomechanical exam

overview: Gait analysis in Kirkland, WA is a close look at how you walk or run. Biomechanics is the science of how your body moves and handles force. Together they help us see why a certain spot hurts. Pain in the foot, shin, knee or hip is sometimes linked to a movement pattern. Finding that pattern can help us choose the right care.

Our visit has two main parts. First, a biomechanical exam checks foot shape, joint motion, strength, flexibility and alignment. Second, we watch you move. We can do gait analysis in person, and we can also use video so we can slow down your motion and look at details. This gives us more information than an exam on the table alone.

Dr. Kate Cryderman has a special interest in biomechanics, and Dr. Lawrence Maurer is a runner who knows how training feels. Many of our patients are runners, but gait review can help walkers, hikers, cyclists and anyone with ongoing pain. People visit us from Kirkland, Totem Lake, Bellevue, Redmond and Seattle. We explain what we see in plain words. You will leave knowing what we found.
symptoms: Foot, shin, knee or hip pain that returns again and again
Pain that begins after a change in shoes, mileage or surface
Shoes that wear out unevenly
Feet that tire fast or feel unstable when you walk or run
An old injury that never felt quite right again
One side that feels different from the other
Pain with no clear cause after rest or other treatment

causes.title: Foot posture
causes.text: Flat feet, high arches and other foot shapes may change how force moves up the leg. A foot that rolls in or stays stiff may add stress to the foot, shin or knee.

causes.title: Joint motion and flexibility
causes.text: A tight calf, a stiff ankle or limited big toe motion may change your stride. The body may find another way to move, which can shift stress to other tissues.

causes.title: Strength and control
causes.text: Weak hips, core or foot muscles may affect balance and control when you land. When muscles tire during a run, your form may change and place more stress on certain areas.

causes.title: Running form
causes.text: Stride length, cadence, foot strike and arm and trunk position can all affect load. Small changes may sometimes reduce strain, but the best form depends on you and your body.

causes.title: Leg length and past injury
causes.text: Differences in leg length or the effects of an old sprain or fracture may change how you move. These patterns can be subtle, and a careful exam can help find them.

diagnosis: A biomechanical exam starts with your story, including pain, activity, past injuries and shoes. We then check foot and ankle shape, motion, strength and balance, and look at alignment from the hips down. Next comes gait analysis. We watch you walk, and we may watch you run, in person and on video. We review the video with you and point out patterns. X-rays or other imaging may be used if the exam suggests a bone or joint problem. Then we explain what we found and what it may mean.

treatments.title: Education about your movement
treatments.text: We show you what we see and explain how it may relate to your pain. Understanding your own movement helps you make better choices about training, shoes and recovery.

treatments.title: Exercises for strength and mobility
treatments.text: Based on your findings, we may suggest exercises for the feet, calves, hips or core. These may help your body control motion better and handle training load.

treatments.title: Gait and running form tips
treatments.text: We may suggest small changes in cadence, stride or posture. These are explained step by step, and we advise changing slowly so your body can adapt.

treatments.title: Shoe and equipment choices
treatments.text: Your shoes can change how you move. We review your footwear and suggest styles that may suit your foot type and activity, including what to look for when you shop.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics when helpful
treatments.text: If foot mechanics are part of the problem, custom orthotics made from a scan or cast of your feet may help guide and support motion. They are not needed for everyone.

treatments.title: Follow-up and referral
treatments.text: We check your progress and adjust the plan. If another type of care may help, such as physical therapy, we can talk about that too. Surgery is rarely the first step.

whenToSeeUs: You have repeat injuries in the same area
Pain comes back every time you increase training
You are starting a running program and want a movement check
You have foot, shin, knee or hip pain with no clear cause
You want to understand how your feet and shoes work together
prevention: Increase your training load slowly and in small steps
Rotate shoes and replace them before they are worn out
Keep your calves, hips, core and feet strong
Mix up surfaces and routes instead of using only one
Get a gait check if you notice new pain patterns after a change in training

faqs.q: What is gait analysis?
faqs.a: Gait analysis is a close look at how you walk or run. We watch your feet, ankles, knees, hips and posture in motion, in person and on video. This helps us see patterns that may relate to pain or injury, and it helps guide choices about exercises, footwear and orthotics.

faqs.q: Do I need to run to get a gait analysis in Kirkland, WA?
faqs.a: No, you do not need to be a runner. Gait analysis can help walkers, hikers and anyone with foot, ankle or leg pain. If you do run, we may watch you run as well. We choose the type of review that fits your activity and your pain.

faqs.q: What is a biomechanical exam?
faqs.a: A biomechanical exam is a hands-on check of how your feet and legs are built and how they move. We look at joint motion, flexibility, strength and alignment, often while you stand and walk. The results help explain why you hurt and help us plan care.

faqs.q: What should I bring to a gait analysis visit?
faqs.a: Bring the shoes you use most, especially running or walking shoes. Wear comfortable clothes that let us see your legs, such as shorts. If you have orthotics, old shoes or past imaging, bring those too. Be ready to share your training habits and any past injuries.

faqs.q: Can changing how I run stop my pain?
faqs.a: Changing how you run may help some people, but results vary. Pain often has more than one cause, such as load, strength, shoes and foot structure. We look at the whole picture and suggest changes slowly. We cannot promise any one change will remove pain.

title: Shin Splints
metaTitle: Shin Splints Treatment for Runners in Kirkland | Run Doctor

h1: Shin Splints Treatment for Runners in Kirkland, WA
summary: Shin splints cause pain along the inner edge of the shin, often after running or sudden changes in training. Our Kirkland team looks for the cause and builds a plan to ease pain and rebuild.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Runners, dancers, hikers and new exercisers

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Aching along the inner shin during activity

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Cut back load and book an exam

overview: Shin splints treatment for runners starts with understanding what is causing the pain. Shin splints, often called medial tibial stress syndrome, is pain along the inner edge of the shin bone. It often shows up when training grows too fast, or when you switch shoes or surfaces. It is common in runners, but hikers, dancers and soccer players can get it too.

The pain can start as a dull ache at the start of a run and ease as you warm up. Over time, it may last longer or hurt even when you walk. Shin splints are not the same as a stress fracture, and the two can feel alike. That is why a careful exam matters, especially if one spot is very tender.

At Run Doctor in Kirkland, we look at your training, your shoes and how your feet and legs move. Dr. Maurer and Dr. Cryderman treat many runners from Kirkland, Totem Lake, Bellevue, Redmond and Woodinville. Care is usually conservative, with load changes, strength work and shoe advice. Orthotics may help some people. Surgery is rarely needed. You will get a clear plan.
symptoms: Dull or sharp aching along the inner edge of the shin
Pain at the start of a run that may ease as you warm up
Tenderness when you press along the shin bone
Mild swelling in the lower leg in some cases
Pain that lasts longer after activity as the problem builds
Pain when walking, climbing stairs or standing after hard training
One very sharp, small spot of pain, which may need to be checked for a stress fracture

causes.title: Too much, too soon
causes.text: A fast jump in mileage, speed, hills or jumping can overload the tissues around the shin. Pain often starts a week or two after a big change in training.

causes.title: Hard or uneven surfaces
causes.text: Running on pavement, a banked road or a hard indoor floor can add stress. A new surface can also be a trigger, because your legs have not adapted to it yet.

causes.title: Shoes that are worn or do not fit
causes.text: Worn out running shoes may lose cushion and support. Shoes that do not suit your foot shape or running style may also add stress to the shin.

causes.title: Foot mechanics
causes.text: Flat feet, high arches or a foot that rolls in a lot may change how force moves through the lower leg. This may add strain to the muscles and bone lining along the shin.

causes.title: Weak or tight muscles
causes.text: Tight calves, weak hips, or weak foot and ankle muscles may change your stride. When muscles tire, the shin may take on more of the work.

diagnosis: We start by asking about your training, shoes, surfaces and when the pain began. Then we examine your shin, feet and ankles, check where it is tender and test strength and flexibility. We watch your gait, in person and sometimes on video, and look at your foot posture and alignment. If we think you may have a stress fracture, or if the pain does not fit shin splints, we may order imaging such as an X-ray or other tests. We then explain what we think is going on and what to do next.

treatments.title: Relative rest and load changes
treatments.text: You may not have to stop all activity. We often suggest cutting back mileage or intensity and adding low impact cross training such as cycling or swimming while the shin settles.

treatments.title: Gradual return to running
treatments.text: When pain allows, we give you a step-by-step plan to build up again. Slow, steady progress helps your body adapt and may lower the chance that pain returns.

treatments.title: Strength and flexibility work
treatments.text: Exercises for the calf, foot, ankle and hip may help the lower leg handle load. We show you what to do and how to progress safely.

treatments.title: Shoe review and replacement
treatments.text: We check the age and fit of your running shoes. Shoes with the right fit and enough life left may reduce stress on the shin, and we can talk about styles to consider.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics when helpful
treatments.text: If foot mechanics seem to add to your pain, orthotics made from a scan or cast of your feet may help support the foot. They are not needed for every runner.

treatments.title: Further tests and options
treatments.text: If pain does not improve with good conservative care, or a stress fracture is possible, we may use imaging and adjust the plan. Surgery is rarely needed and is a last resort.

whenToSeeUs: Shin pain has lasted more than one to two weeks
Pain hurts at rest or at night
You have one spot that is very tender to the touch
Pain is getting worse even though you have cut back
You have swelling, numbness or tingling in the leg or foot
prevention: Raise mileage and intensity slowly, in small steps
Replace running shoes before they are worn out
Vary surfaces and avoid running only on hard ground
Strengthen your calves, feet and hips
Warm up before runs and pay attention to early shin aches

faqs.q: What is the best shin splints treatment for runners?
faqs.a: The best care often starts with reducing training load, then rebuilding slowly. Cross training, strength work, good shoes and sometimes orthotics may help. The right plan depends on the cause, so a visit helps. We look at your training, shoes and movement before suggesting a plan.

faqs.q: How long do shin splints take to heal?
faqs.a: It varies. Mild cases may settle in a few weeks with less load, while longer problems may take more time. Returning too soon is a common reason pain comes back. We give you a step-by-step plan, and we cannot promise an exact time frame.

faqs.q: Can I keep running with shin splints?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but it depends on your pain. Mild pain that settles quickly may allow reduced running, while sharp or lasting pain suggests you should stop and get checked. Cross training such as cycling or swimming may help you stay active while the shin recovers.

faqs.q: How do I tell shin splints from a stress fracture?
faqs.a: They can feel alike, so an exam matters. Shin splints are often a wider ache along the shin, while a stress fracture often hurts in one small spot and may hurt at rest or at night. If you suspect a fracture, see a podiatrist for an exam and imaging if needed.

faqs.q: Do shin splints need surgery?
faqs.a: Almost never. Most people improve with conservative care such as load changes, strength work, shoe advice and gradual return to running. Surgery is only a last resort for rare cases that do not respond to a long course of good care. We discuss all options with you.

h1: Ankle Sprain and Fracture Treatment in Kirkland, WA
summary: Foot and ankle trauma includes sprains, fractures and other sudden injuries. Our Kirkland team can examine the injury, explain your options and guide healing, while serious emergencies need the ER.

quickFacts.label: Common injuries
quickFacts.value: Ankle sprains, fractures, strains and ligament injuries

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Sudden pain, swelling and trouble putting weight on the foot

quickFacts.label: Emergency
quickFacts.value: Call 911 or go to the ER for severe injury

overview: Ankle sprain fracture treatment in Kirkland starts with finding out how serious the injury is. Foot and ankle trauma means a sudden injury such as a twisted ankle, a fall, a landing from a jump or a hit to the foot. These injuries can involve ligaments, tendons, muscles or bones. Some are mild, and others need prompt care. You will get a clear plan.

An ankle sprain is a stretch or tear of the ligaments that hold the ankle steady. A fracture is a break in a bone. They can look alike at first, with pain, swelling and bruising. You cannot always tell by how it feels. A proper exam, and often an X-ray, helps us tell the difference and choose the right care.

Run Doctor in Kirkland treats foot and ankle injuries for athletes and non-athletes. Dr. Lawrence Maurer is a foot and ankle surgeon, and both of our doctors focus on conservative care first. Surgery is discussed only when it is the best option. Patients come from Totem Lake, Bellevue, Redmond, Bothell, Woodinville and Seattle. If you have an emergency, go to the ER first.
symptoms: Sudden pain after a twist, fall, landing or direct hit
Swelling that develops soon after the injury
Bruising around the ankle, foot or toes
Pain when you try to stand or walk on the foot
Tenderness over a bone or along the ankle
A feeling of the ankle giving way
A pop or snap at the time of the injury

causes.title: Rolling or twisting the ankle
causes.text: Stepping on uneven ground, landing on another player's foot or turning quickly can force the ankle past its normal range. This is the most common cause of sprains.

causes.title: Falls and impact
causes.text: A fall, a drop from a height or a hard landing can break a bone or injure ligaments. Heavy objects or direct hits to the foot may also cause fractures.

causes.title: Sports and activity
causes.text: Soccer, basketball, trail running, hiking and skiing all carry a risk of sudden foot and ankle injury, especially on uneven ground or during fast direction changes.

causes.title: Weak or unstable ankles
causes.text: A past sprain, weak muscles or poor balance may make the ankle more likely to roll again. Repeat sprains can lead to ongoing instability if they are not treated well.

causes.title: Footwear and surfaces
causes.text: Shoes that do not give enough support, worn soles, wet trails or uneven ground can all raise the risk of a twist or fall.

diagnosis: We begin by asking how the injury happened and what you felt. Then we examine the foot and ankle, looking at swelling, bruising, tender spots, motion, stability and your ability to bear weight. We often use an X-ray to check for a fracture, and we may suggest other imaging if we think ligaments, tendons or cartilage are hurt. We also check for signs of nerve or blood flow problems. After the exam, we explain what we found, how serious it is and what steps to take.

treatments.title: Protection and support
treatments.text: Depending on the injury, we may use a brace, boot, splint or crutches to protect the area. This helps it heal in a good position and limits further damage.

treatments.title: Swelling control
treatments.text: Elevation, compression and other measures may help control swelling in the early days after an injury. We tell you what is safe and helpful for your specific injury.

treatments.title: Casting or immobilization for fractures
treatments.text: Many foot and ankle fractures heal with a boot or cast and time off the foot. We explain how long to protect it and when we will check your progress.

treatments.title: Rehabilitation and balance training
treatments.text: After the early healing phase, exercises for motion, strength and balance help the ankle recover. This work may lower the chance of repeat sprains. We show you each step.

treatments.title: Return to activity plan
treatments.text: We help you build back to walking, running or sport in steps. Going back too fast can set healing back, so we guide you based on how the injury is doing.

treatments.title: Surgery when needed
treatments.text: Some fractures or severe ligament injuries need surgery, such as when bones are out of place or the ankle is unstable. Dr. Maurer is a foot and ankle surgeon and will explain every option.

whenToSeeUs: Emergency: call 911 or go to the ER for a bone sticking through the skin, a foot that looks badly out of shape, heavy bleeding, a cold or pale foot, or loss of feeling
Go to the ER or urgent care if you cannot bear any weight, or the injury came from a major fall or crash
Book a visit soon for ongoing swelling, bruising or pain after a sprain
See us if the ankle keeps giving way or you have repeat sprains
See us for pain that is not improving after a few days of careful rest
prevention: Wear shoes that fit well and give good support for your activity
Do balance and ankle strength exercises, especially after a past sprain
Warm up before sports and take care on uneven ground
Use caution on wet, icy or loose surfaces
Rehab an injury fully before returning to full sport

faqs.q: How do I know if my ankle is sprained or broken?
faqs.a: You cannot be sure without an exam. Both injuries can cause pain, swelling and bruising. Signs that suggest a break include pain over a bone, a foot that looks out of shape, or trouble bearing any weight. An exam and X-ray can tell the difference, so get it checked.

faqs.q: When should I go to the ER for a foot or ankle injury?
faqs.a: Call 911 or go to the ER right away for a bone through the skin, an obviously deformed foot, heavy bleeding, a cold, pale or blue foot, numbness, or an injury from a major fall or crash. Also go if you cannot bear any weight. These are emergencies, not office visits.

faqs.q: How long does an ankle sprain take to heal?
faqs.a: It varies with how bad the sprain is. Mild sprains may settle in a few weeks, while more serious ones may take longer. Rehab and balance work are important, since healing does not always mean the ankle is strong again. We guide you through each stage and give a plan.

faqs.q: Can a fracture heal without surgery?
faqs.a: Yes, many foot and ankle fractures heal without surgery with a boot, cast or other protection and time. Some need surgery, such as when bones are out of place or the joint is unstable. We examine the injury, review the X-ray and explain what is best for you.

faqs.q: Do you treat ankle sprains and fractures in Kirkland?
faqs.a: Yes. Run Doctor in Kirkland evaluates and treats foot and ankle injuries, including sprains and fractures. We use conservative care first, and Dr. Maurer is a foot and ankle surgeon if surgery is needed. For severe injuries, go to the ER first, then call us for follow-up care.

h1: Foot Problems and Low Back Pain in Kirkland, WA
summary: How your feet move can affect your ankles, knees, hips and back. Our Kirkland podiatrists check your foot mechanics and gait, and we also advise seeing your primary doctor about back pain.

quickFacts.label: Possible link
quickFacts.value: Foot mechanics, gait, knees, hips and low back

quickFacts.value: Back, hip or knee pain along with foot issues

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: A foot and gait exam, plus your primary doctor

overview: Foot problems and low back pain may be linked for some people. Your feet are your base when you stand, walk and run. If they move in an uneven way, the forces may travel up through the ankles, knees, hips and back. This does not mean your feet cause your back pain. It means foot mechanics may be one piece of the puzzle.

Back pain has many causes, such as muscle strain, joint problems, disc problems, posture, work habits and more. That is why we do not promise that foot care will fix back pain. What we can do is check whether your feet and gait add stress to the body, and treat foot problems that may be part of the picture. We will tell you honestly what we find.

At Run Doctor in Kirkland, we look at your feet, ankles and how you walk. Dr. Kate Cryderman has a special interest in biomechanics, and our care starts with conservative steps. We also recommend you see your primary doctor for back pain, especially if you have red flag signs. Patients come from Kirkland, Bellevue, Redmond, Bothell and Seattle. You will get a clear plan.
symptoms: Low back, hip or knee pain along with foot or arch pain
Back or leg tiredness after standing or walking for a while
Flat feet or high arches along with ongoing body aches
Shoes that wear unevenly
One foot or leg that seems to turn out or roll in more than the other
Pain that changes when you change shoes or surfaces
Foot pain that makes you change how you walk

causes.title: Foot posture
causes.text: Flat feet or very high arches may change how force passes up the leg. Some people notice more strain in the knees, hips or back, though the link is not the same for everyone.

causes.title: Changed walking pattern
causes.text: Foot pain can make you limp or shift your weight. Over time, this changed pattern may add stress to the hips and back, even after the foot problem is mild.

causes.title: Leg length differences
causes.text: A small difference in leg length, or how the feet are built, may affect balance and hip level. Whether it matters depends on the person and needs a careful exam.

causes.title: Stiff or weak parts of the chain
causes.text: A tight calf, a stiff ankle or weak hips can change how the body moves. The back may take on extra load when other areas do not move or support well.

causes.title: Other back causes
causes.text: Many back problems have nothing to do with the feet. Muscle strain, joints, discs, posture, work habits or other health issues can all cause pain, which is why your primary doctor should check it.

diagnosis: We begin by asking about your foot and back symptoms, your daily activity and your shoes. Then we do a biomechanical exam, checking foot shape, joint motion, strength and alignment from the hips to the feet. We watch your gait, in person and often on video. We may order imaging for foot or ankle problems if needed. We do not diagnose back disease, so we also suggest you see your primary doctor for back pain. Then we explain what we found and whether foot mechanics may play a part.

treatments.title: Treating foot problems
treatments.text: If you have a foot problem such as plantar fasciitis or flat feet, we treat that first. Easing foot pain may help you walk in a more even way.

treatments.title: Gait and movement review
treatments.text: We show you what we see in your walking pattern. This may help you understand how your feet, hips and legs work together and what to work on.

treatments.title: Strength and mobility exercises
treatments.text: Exercises for the feet, calves and hips may help your body support itself. Your primary doctor or a physical therapist may advise back specific exercises.

treatments.title: Footwear advice
treatments.text: Supportive shoes that fit well may help comfort during standing and walking. We help you choose styles that match your foot type and daily needs.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics when helpful
treatments.text: If foot mechanics seem to add stress, orthotics made from a scan or cast of your feet may help support the foot. They may help some people, and we cannot promise a change in back pain.

treatments.title: Teamwork with your other doctors
treatments.text: We suggest working with your primary doctor, and with a physical therapist if advised. Back pain often needs more than one kind of care. We are glad to share notes.

whenToSeeUs: You have foot, arch or heel pain along with back, hip or knee pain
You have flat feet or high arches and ongoing aches in the legs or back
Your shoes wear unevenly and you want to know why
You have changed how you walk because of foot pain
Red flag back symptoms need a primary doctor or ER first: numbness in the groin, loss of bladder or bowel control, weakness in the legs, fever, or pain after a major injury
prevention: Treat foot pain early so it does not change how you walk
Wear shoes that fit well and replace them when they are worn
Keep your calves, hips and core strong and flexible
Move often if you stand or sit for long hours
See your primary doctor when back pain lasts or keeps returning

faqs.q: Can foot problems cause low back pain?
faqs.a: They may contribute for some people, but they are not the only cause. Foot posture and gait can change how force moves through the knees, hips and back. Back pain has many other causes, so we check your feet and also advise you to see your primary doctor.

faqs.q: Will orthotics fix my back pain?
faqs.a: We cannot promise that. Orthotics may help some people by supporting the foot and changing how force travels up the leg, but back pain has many causes. We use orthotics when your exam shows foot mechanics may play a part, and we explain what to expect.

faqs.q: Should I see a podiatrist or my primary doctor for back pain?
faqs.a: Start with your primary doctor for back pain, since many causes are not in the feet. A podiatrist can help if you also have foot problems, flat feet, high arches or gait concerns. The two kinds of care can work together, and we are happy to share information.

faqs.q: What back pain symptoms need urgent care?
faqs.a: Go to the ER or call your doctor right away for numbness in the groin or inner thighs, loss of bladder or bowel control, new leg weakness, fever with back pain, or pain after a major fall or crash. These can be serious and need prompt medical care.

faqs.q: How can my gait affect my hips and knees in Kirkland or anywhere?
faqs.a: Your gait sets how force moves through your joints with each step. If your foot rolls in a lot or stays stiff, the ankle, knee and hip may share extra load. Our Kirkland team can review your gait and foot mechanics, though results vary by person.

h1: Arthritis Foot and Ankle Treatment in Kirkland, WA
summary: Arthritis can make the joints of the foot and ankle stiff, swollen and sore. Our Kirkland team offers supportive care such as bracing and footwear advice to help you stay active and comfortable.

quickFacts.label: Types
quickFacts.value: Osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Stiff, sore or swollen joints, worse after rest

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: An exam, with imaging when needed

overview: Arthritis foot and ankle treatment in Kirkland begins with knowing which kind of arthritis you have. Arthritis means joint inflammation or wear. Your foot has many small joints, and the ankle and big toe take a lot of load every day. When these joints become sore and stiff, simple things like walking, standing or hiking may feel harder. You will get a clear plan.

Osteoarthritis is often linked to wear over time or an old injury. Inflammatory types, such as rheumatoid arthritis or psoriatic arthritis, involve the immune system and may affect other joints too. They are managed with your primary doctor or a rheumatologist. We focus on the foot and ankle and work with your other doctors when needed. We explain each type in plain words.

Care at Run Doctor is conservative first. We help with supportive footwear, bracing, orthotics, activity changes and in-office options. A physician may talk about injections in some cases. Surgery is a last resort when other care has not helped. Dr. Maurer is a foot and ankle surgeon. Patients visit us from Kirkland, Totem Lake, Bellevue, Redmond and Seattle. We take time to explain each choice.
symptoms: Aching or stiffness in the foot, ankle or big toe joint
Pain that is worse after rest and eases a bit with movement
Swelling or warmth around a joint
A grinding feeling or reduced range of motion
Bumps or bone spurs near the joints
Pain with walking, stairs or standing for long periods
Changes in how a joint looks over time

causes.title: Wear and tear
causes.text: Over many years, the cartilage that cushions a joint may thin. This is called osteoarthritis. It often affects the big toe joint, midfoot and ankle.

causes.title: Past injury
causes.text: A sprain, fracture or other joint injury may change how the joint moves. Years later, this can lead to arthritis in the foot or ankle in some people.

causes.title: Inflammatory arthritis
causes.text: Conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and gout can inflame the joints. They may affect the feet early and often need care from a primary doctor or rheumatologist.

causes.title: Foot structure and alignment
causes.text: Flat feet, high arches or uneven alignment may place more stress on certain joints. Over time, this extra load may add to joint wear in some people.

causes.title: Family history and age
causes.text: Arthritis is more common as we get older, and it may run in families. These are not things you can change, but supportive care can still help you stay active.

diagnosis: We start with your story: where it hurts, how long it has been, what makes it better or worse, and any past injuries or arthritis diagnosis. We examine your feet and ankles, checking joint motion, swelling, alignment and how you walk. X-rays are often used to see the joint space and any bone changes. Other imaging or lab tests may be suggested if we think an inflammatory type may be involved. We then explain what we found and share findings with your primary doctor or rheumatologist when it helps.

treatments.title: Supportive footwear
treatments.text: Shoes with good cushion, a stiff or rocker sole and a roomy toe box may reduce stress on sore joints. We help you choose styles that suit your feet.

treatments.title: Bracing and orthotics
treatments.text: Ankle braces or custom orthotics made from a scan or cast of your feet may help support joints and spread out pressure. We match the support to the joint that is affected.

treatments.title: Activity changes
treatments.text: Low impact choices such as cycling or swimming may be easier on the joints than running. We help you find a balance that keeps you active while limiting flare-ups.

treatments.title: Exercises and mobility work
treatments.text: Gentle exercises may help keep joints moving and muscles strong. We suggest safe options and may talk about working with a physical therapist. We keep it simple and safe.

treatments.title: In-office options, including injections
treatments.text: Depending on your case, a physician may discuss options such as an injection into a joint. This is something to talk about together, not a promise of results, and it is not right for everyone.

treatments.title: Surgery as a last resort
treatments.text: If pain limits daily life and other care has not helped, a surgeon may talk about options. These may include joint procedures. We explain risks, benefits and recovery before any decision.

whenToSeeUs: Joint pain or stiffness in the foot or ankle lasts more than a few weeks
A joint is red, hot, very swollen or suddenly very painful, which needs prompt care
You have trouble walking or doing daily tasks because of joint pain
You have arthritis elsewhere and now notice foot symptoms
Footwear and over-the-counter products are not giving you enough comfort
prevention: Keep a healthy, active routine with low impact exercise
Wear supportive shoes with enough room for your toes
Treat foot and ankle injuries fully and early
Stretch and move the joints gently each day
Keep up with care for any inflammatory condition with your primary doctor

faqs.q: What is the best arthritis foot and ankle treatment?
faqs.a: There is no single best treatment. Most people start with supportive footwear, activity changes, bracing or orthotics, and gentle exercise. The right plan depends on the joint and the type of arthritis. We examine you, review your imaging and suggest steps to help you stay comfortable and active.

faqs.q: What is the difference between osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis?
faqs.a: Osteoarthritis is joint wear, often tied to age or past injury. Inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, comes from the immune system and may affect many joints. Care for inflammatory types is usually shared with a primary doctor or rheumatologist, while we focus on the foot and ankle.

faqs.q: Do orthotics and braces help arthritic feet?
faqs.a: They may help some people. Orthotics and braces can support a joint, spread out pressure and limit painful motion. Results vary, and not everyone needs them. We choose a device based on which joint hurts and how you walk, and we adjust the plan if needed.

faqs.q: Are injections used for foot or ankle arthritis?
faqs.a: Injections may be one option a physician discusses in some cases, but they are not right for everyone. We review your exam, imaging and goals first. If an injection is a fit, we explain what it may and may not do, along with risks, before you decide.

faqs.q: Do I need surgery for foot or ankle arthritis?
faqs.a: Most people do not need surgery. Conservative care such as footwear, bracing, orthotics and activity changes is tried first. Surgery may be discussed as a last resort if pain limits your life and other care has not helped. We explain every option before you decide.
